The teenager had joined the student demonstrations that forced the former Education minister Dharmendra Pradhan to resign. Like many young protesters around her, she directed her ire at Prime Minister Narendra Modi. A video clip of her comments went viral. Then came the targeted harassment campaign. items.summary: In May 2020, as India was preparing to overhaul its education policy, the Narendra Modi government held a review meeting on education that placed technology at the centre, to help build what the government described as a “global knowledge super power”. Two months later, the Union Cabinet approved the National Education Policy. It made digital literacy, coding and computational thinking essential skills for every student. Coding activities were proposed to begin in the middle stage (Grades 6–8), while mathematics and computational thinking had to receive stronger focus from the foundational years. In September that year, PM Modi spoke about what education should look like in the 21st century – from coding to artificial intelligence, the Internet of Things, cloud computing, data science and robotics. But five years later, the latest 2025-26 UDISE+ (Unified District Information System for Education Plus) data presents a stark picture on digital awareness inside India’s schools. UDISE+ describes itself as the Ministry of Education’s official school education information system and says its data is collected from recognised schools and validated through administrative levels. items.title: BJP promises ‘positive content’. Its new social media team’s record tells another story

We have been creating positive content and taking it to people. I will try to add momentum to this.” The 58-year-old chemistry professor-turned-politician has spent over a decade in the party’s IT cell. While he accused the Opposition of peddling “fake narratives” and promised to fight them with “positive content”, his own state unit’s Instagram account was busy dividing Gen Z into communal categories. Three weeks before his appointment, the BJP’s Chhattisgarh unit posted a reel juxtaposing an Instagram creator’s video from a Mumbai protest against NEET-UG paper leaks with footage of a student receiving an award from President Droupadi Murmu. One of the biggest changes was the leadership’s decision to drop Amit Malviya as national social media convenor and replace him with Mhaske. items.summary: The Gauhati High Court recently closed a public interest litigation (PIL) petition filed seeking uniform guidelines on adjournments and mandatory digital upload of court records. A Division Bench of Justices Michael Zothankhuma and Arun Dev Choudhury on August 10 noted that the petitioner himself submitted that an intervening administrative notification issued by the High Court Registry had addressed the concerns raised in the matter. "Mr. R. Justice Michael Zothankhuma Reetam Singh, an advocate enrolled with the Bar Council of Assam, Nagaland, Mizoram, Arunachal Pradesh and Sikkim, had filed the PIL in 2024. He cited his own experience in a case filed under the Negotiable Instruments Act and a money suit to argue that adjournments were being routinely granted by trial courts on inadequate grounds. These measures were intended to ensure transparency for litigants who otherwise depend entirely on their counsel for information about case proceedings. The petition also sought the constitution of a committee to frame adjournment guidelines, a digital date-allocation system to be developed in consultation with technical experts from IIT Guwahati, and the framing of disciplinary rules against counsel who misuse the adjournment process. items.title: Supreme Court restores Congress leader’s election petition challenging BJP MP Kripanath Mallah’s 2024 poll win
items.summary: The Supreme Court on Monday set aside the Gauhati High Court’s dismissal of an election petition challenging Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) Member of Parliament Kripanath Mallah’s victory in the 2024 Lok Sabha elections. [ Hafiz Rashid Ahmed Choudhury v. Kripanath Mallah and Others ] Congress candidate and Senior Advocate Hafiz Rashid Ahmed Choudhury had challenged Mallah's election on the ground that the BJP leader had employed corrupt practices to win the elections from Assam's Karimganj parliamentary constituency. In April 2025, however, the Gauhati High Court, dismissed Choudhury's petition on noting certain defects in it. The High Court did not go into the merits of the case. A Bench of Justices JB Pardiwala and K Vinod Chandran today allowed Chowdhury's appeal against this ruling. The top court held that the defects cited by the High Court to dismiss Chowdhury's petition at the threshold were not fatal. Justice JB Pardiwala and Justice Vinod Chandran The defect flagged by the High Court concerned a Form 25 affidavit filed by Choudhury in support of his allegations that Mallah had committed corrupt practices. The original affidavit in the High Court’s record appeared to have been affirmed before a commissioner of affidavits. However, the copy served on Mallah did not carry any endorsement showing such affirmation. The top court today held that this omission did not justify dismissing the entire election petition. " Obviously, the defect under Section 83 does not entail peremptory dismissal under Section 86 of the RoP Act ,” the Supreme Court said. Therefore, it directed the High Court to verify whether the original affidavit contained the required attestation. If it did, the High Court was directed to consider the petition on merits, including by examining the allegations of corrupt practices. If the required attestation was absent, the Court said Choudhury should not be permitted to pursue the allegations of corrupt practices. However, the High Court must still examine other independent grounds, if any, raised in the petition, the Supreme Court added. “ Suffice it to request the High Court to verify and if due attestation of the affirmation on oath is available, proceed with the matter on merits and if not available, not to permit the allegation of corrupt practices to be urged and proceed with the consideration on the merits of the other grounds, if any are pleaded ,” the Court said. Mallah had defeated Choudhury by 18,360 votes, a margin of around 1.

items.title: Forensic evidence should aid cases, not create more burden for survivors: Ex-ASG Pinky Anand
items.summary: Better forensic practices should strengthen cases before courts without creating an additional burden of proof for survivors of sexual and gender-based violence, former Additional Solicitor General of India Pinky Anand said at a training workshop in Goa on Saturday. The day-long workshop, held on August 22, focused on implementing Standard Operating Procedures (SOPs) for the collection, preservation, chain of custody and presentation of forensic evidence in cases of sexual assault, rape and child abuse. “Better forensic practice must strengthen the case that reaches the court. It must never become a fresh threshold of belief that survivors are asked to clear,” said Anand. The SOPs were formally launched by Anand at the Police Headquarters in Panjim on April 26 last year, marking World DNA Day. They were subsequently expanded to include the handling of forensic evidence in cases involving child abuse. The workshop brought together police officers, prosecutors, judicial officers, medical practitioners and other professionals involved in the investigation and prosecution of sexual and gender-based violence and child abuse cases. A key focus was a victim-centred approach to investigation. The participants discussed how survivors could be treated with dignity and sensitivity while ensuring that evidence is collected in accordance with due process. The sessions also covered practical aspects of collecting and preserving forensic material, maintaining its chain of custody and presenting it before courts. Medical experts discussed factors affecting the reliability and evidentiary value of forensic material. Legal practitioners examined how such evidence should be presented in court. SOP Training Workshop, Goa Speaking at the workshop, Anand said forensic evidence in sexual violence cases can disappear within hours. She cited instances where a survivor may bathe, clothes may be washed or a crime scene may be cleaned. She stressed that procedural discipline was critical to ensuring forensic evidence could withstand scrutiny in court. " The science was sound throughout; what failed, for a time, was the discipline around it — which is precisely what a Standard Operating Procedure exists to secure, from the first responder at the scene to an unbroken chain of custody that can withstand cross-examination," said Anand. items.title: DPIIT relaxes FDI norms for export-oriented inventory-based e-commerce
items.summary: The Department of Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade, Ministry of Commerce and Industry, Government of India has issued Press Note No. 3 of 2026 dated 23 July 2026 (“Press Note No. 3”), introducing a targeted relaxation to India’s foreign direct investment (“FDI”) policy governing e-commerce activities. Background India’s FDI policy on e-commerce activities has evolved progressively over the last two decades. Press Note No. 2 of 2000 first permitted FDI up to 100% in e-commerce activities. However, such permission was subject to certain conditions and did not extend to retail trading. Accordingly, the permission was limited to companies engaged in business-to-business e-commerce. Recognising the rapid growth of digital commerce, Press Note No. 3 of 2016 introduced a distinction between the marketplace model and the inventory-based model of e-commerce. While FDI continued to remain impermissible in the inventory-based model of e-commerce, up to 100% FDI under the automatic route was permitted in the marketplace model. An inventory-based model of e-commerce refers to an e-commerce activity where the inventory of goods or services is owned by the e-commerce entity and sold directly to consumers. In contrast, the marketplace model refers to the provision of an information technology platform by an e-commerce entity on a digital and electronic network to facilitate transactions between buyers and sellers. Press Note No. 2 of 2018 clarified what constitutes ownership or control over inventory. The inventory of a vendor would be deemed to be controlled by an e-commerce marketplace entity when more than 25% of the vendor’s purchases are from the marketplace entity or its group companies. Accordingly, ownership or control over inventory would render the business an inventory-based model, thereby attracting the relevant provisions of the FDI policy. What has changed? Press Note No. 3 inserts a new paragraph 5.2.15.2.5 in the FDI policy permitting an e-commerce entity to engage in an inventory-based model solely for the export of goods/products manufactured and/or produced in India. The amendment further clarifies that the existing restrictions applicable to business-to-consumer and inventory-based e-commerce shall not apply to these export transactions. Accordingly, e-commerce entities with FDI may now procure, own, warehouse and export goods manufactured and/or produced in India directly to overseas customers. items.title: When debtors hold on to the wheel: A comparative perspective on India’s CIIRP and Singapore’s Scheme of Arrangement
items.summary: Every rescue regime answers one question first: who controls the company while its financial distress is addressed? India’s newly introduced Creditor-Initiated Insolvency Resolution Process (“CIIRP”), inserted as Chapter IV-A of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 (“IBC”), answers that question through a hybrid model: creditors initiate the process, but the company’s management remains in control, not the creditors who triggered it. The management can lead the restructuring process subject to the supervision of a resolution professional (“RP”). It intentionally sits between India’s two existing regimes — the Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process (“CIRP”), which is creditor-driven and displaces management on admission, and the Pre-Packaged Insolvency Resolution Process, which preserves debtor control but only for micro, small and medium enterprises. Singapore’s scheme of arrangement — a court-supervised compromise between a company and its creditors — operates in a similar vein. The company’s management remains in control by default, creditors vote on a compromise proposed by the company, and the court’s role is focused on integrity of the process and procedural discipline rather than the commercial bargain proposed for the restructuring. The result is a debtor-in-possession model close enough to India’s CIIRP. Both the CIIRP and Singapore’s scheme of arrangement share a staged structure. Where the law on CIIRP can rely on ten years of extensive precedents created by Indian insolvency tribunals for CIRP cases, it still leaves open some new questions that may see litigation in the first wave of cases. Singapore’s answers to these questions were tested by a specialist court and a decade of appellate decisions and may serve as a reference point. items.title: Can contractual clauses mandate pre-deposit before arbitration? Supreme Court refers issue to larger bench
items.summary: The Supreme Court has doubted the correctness of its own ruling upholding arbitration clauses that require only contractors to deposit a percentage of their claim before invoking arbitration [Santosh Associate v. HSIIDC]. A Bench of Justices Manoj Misra and Manmohan asked the Chief Justice of India to consider referring the issue to a larger bench. Justice Manmohan and Justice Manoj Misra Accordingly, the Bench requested the Chief Justice of India to consider referring a set of questions to a larger bench. These include: • Whether a clause requiring only the contractor to make a pre-deposit before arbitration violates Section 18 of the Arbitration Act, which mandates equal treatment of both parties at every stage of arbitration. • Whether pre-deposit conditions discourage parties from turning to arbitration in the first place, defeating its purpose of easing the burden on courts. • Whether such a condition is arbitrary and violates the right to sue, Article 14 of the Constitution and Section 28 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872. • Whether requiring a pre-deposit has any real connection to the goal of weeding out frivolous claims, given that frivolous claims can already be addressed through costs at the end of arbitration under Section 31(8) of the Arbitration Act. • Whether a pre-deposit clause is valid if the deposit is refundable once arbitration concludes. • Whether SK Jain continues to be a valid, binding precedent at all. The Court was hearing an appeal by a party whose claim was dismissed after it refused to deposit 10% of its claim amount, a requirement under its contract with the Haryana State Industrial and Infrastructure Development Corporation. The dispute arose from a drainage works contract awarded to Santosh Associate Private Limited in 2017. The contract contained a clause requiring the contractor, if it wished to raise a claim exceeding ₹1 lakh, to deposit 10% of the claim amount as security before the dispute could go to arbitration. When the contractor sought arbitration over payment disputes after the contract’s scope was later reduced, the Corporation objected, citing the contractor’s failure to make this deposit. The arbitrator upheld the objection and dismissed the claim in its entirety when the contractor refused to pay. A commercial court in Gurugram later upheld this dismissal, relying on the Supreme Court’s 2009 ruling in SK Jain v. State of Haryana , which had upheld a similar clause. items.title: Understanding the intelligence pyramid: Why most businesses know everything and do nothing?
items.summary: In every consequential field of human endeavour, whether in the boardroom, the courtroom, or on the trading floor, one resource has consistently separated those who prevail from those who do not. The resource is intelligence: information that has been processed, placed in context, and converted into a decision within the window in which that decision still counts. Military history makes the point plainly. The intelligence failures that determined the outcomes of wars were rarely failures of collection; the signals were usually present. What failed was the architecture to convert those signals into understanding, and the discipline to act before the moment passed. Corporate history repeats the lesson, and increasingly, so does the law. When a regulator, a court, or a shareholder examines how an organisation behaved before a loss crystallised, the question is seldom whether the information existed. It is whether the organisation recognised what it held and converted that knowledge into a reasoned, recorded decision, or allowed it to travel no further than the report in which it arrived. In India, Section 166 of the Companies Act, 2013 requires directors to act in good faith and to exercise due and reasonable care, skill, and diligence, a standard against which a board's conduct is later assessed with the benefit of hindsight. This framing is more instructive. And it is the framing of the Intelligence Pyramid , a framework developed by IIRIS, that is designed to address. Directors' duties and the architecture of decision-making The Intelligence Pyramid categorizes enterprise intelligence into three levels: Strategic, Tactical, and Operational . The basic principle behind the intelligence pyramid is that intelligence needs to flow continuously and bidirectionally through all three levels. The minute that process gets broken down due to departmental silos, conflicting incentives, or poor infrastructure, it is not just an issue of becoming less responsive but one of creating liabilities. It encompasses domains such as Regulatory and Compliance Foresight, M&A and Strategic Alliance Intelligence, and Insider Threat Intelligence. These are the areas through which boards anticipate regulatory change, evaluate strategic opportunities, and identify emerging risks. items.title: Who will lead India’s next student movement? | What's Your Ism? EP 54
items.summary: Student politics is returning to the centre of India’s political conversation. But what does this new wave of student activism stand for, and can it grow into a broader political movement? Listen & follow on Youtube Listen & follow on Apple Listen & follow on Spotify In this episode of What's Your ISM?, The News Minute Executive Editor Sudipto Mondal sits down with student leaders from the All India Students’ Association (AISA) and Ambedkar Students’ Association (ASA) to discuss the new opportunities to build student politics, the growing anger on Indian campuses, and the possibilities and contradictions within today’s student movements. Sudipto and the student leaders also explore the relationship between caste and class politics, Ambedkar and Marx, the Left and Ambedkarite movements, and whether these forces can find common ground. They discuss the recent student protests, the rise of Gen Z politics, the education crisis, privatisation, unemployment, and the demand for student union elections in Karnataka. The conversation also looks at whether student organisations can build a third front beyond the BJP and Congress, the challenges of organising across caste and class lines, and the role of ideology in sustaining a movement beyond a single protest. They also discuss the Rohith Act campaign in Karnataka, and how different student organisations came together to push for stronger protections against discrimination in universities. items.title: Editors Guild condemns BJP for calling Rajdeep Sardesai and others ‘Dimaagi Naxals’
items.summary: The Editors Guild of India (EGI) has strongly condemned the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) for targeting individuals who have questioned the government, particularly senior journalist and former Guild president Rajdeep Sardesai, by labelling him a “Dimaagi Naxal” (person with a Naxal mentality). The Guild’s condemnation comes after the BJP’s Goa unit shared an AI-generated video song titled “Who is a Dimaagi Naxal?”, in which several prominent critics of the government are depicted alongside imagery of guns and violence. The video has raised concerns not merely over the use of political labels, but over the threatening and potentially intimidating manner in which the BJP has portrayed people it identifies as its ideological opponents. The BJP’s Goa unit captioned the video: “Violence gets intellectualised, Terrorists get sympathised with, Soldiers get interrogated. If that sounds familiar, you know who you are.” The AI-generated rap video opens with an illustration of Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) leader Abhijeet Dipke. As his head is shown opening, an AK-47 pops out, explicitly associating him with the “Dimaagi Naxal” label. The video then features Congress leader Rahul Gandhi and visuals from CJP protests, accompanied by lyrics accusing “Dimaagi Naxals” of glorifying armed rebellion, sympathising with terrorists and questioning security forces. It also targets Muslims. The video goes further, naming and depicting several political opponents, activists, actors and journalists, including CJP leaders Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka, as well as Prakash Raj, Vishal Dadlani and Arvind Kejriwal. At one point, an AK-47 is shown firing at the people featured in the video. The video concludes with images of Vishal Dadlani, journalist Dhruv Rathee, Rahul Gandhi, Arvind Kejriwal, Rajdeep Sardesai and Prakash Raj, all depicted with bloodied eyes, as if the gun had fired through their temples. items.title: Jaipur Dialogues —a platform that doxxed 15-year-old protestor—has BJP ties
items.summary: In late July 2026, an online storm upended the life of a 15-year-old girl. The teenager had joined the student demonstrations that forced the former Education minister Dharmendra Pradhan to resign. Like many young protesters around her, she directed her ire at Prime Minister Narendra Modi. A video clip of her comments went viral. Then came the targeted harassment campaign. Leading the charge was an organisation called The Jaipur Dialogues. Founded by Sanjay Dixit, a former Indian Administrative Services officer, it describes itself as a “vibrant online platform that aims to promote Indic knowledge systems.” In a series of posts on X, The Jaipur Dialogues’ handle sought the girl’s identifying details, branded her “most wanted”, and eventually, doxxed her. The 15-year-old protester faced threats of rape, murder, and acid attacks. Strangers showed up at her home. Her family and she went into hiding. The Jaipur Dialogues defended its actions as those of a “responsible nationalist platform” in an article it published on August 1. “We posted those images on our X handle, demanded public identification of those who crossed every line of decency, and were fully prepared to back legal action,” the article said . “If demanding accountability for open contempt of the Prime Minister of India makes Jaipur Dialogues guilty in the eyes of the left, we wear that guilt proudly.” The organisation’s conduct towards the teenager brought its wider content under scrutiny. The Jaipur Dialogues’ website—which has sections such as “Islam” and “Sanatana”—publishes stories that are often propagandist and communal. Consider some recent examples: a piece that is headlined “Demographic Jihad claims another locality in Gujarat”, and another that frames Tamil Nadu Chief Minister Vijay’s decision to challenge the state ban on cow slaughter as a “blatant nod to minority vote-bank appeasement”. items.title: Karnataka records 4,212 influenza cases; Health Dept says H1N1 rise is seasonal
items.summary: Karnataka has recorded 4,212 laboratory-confirmed influenza cases across 32 districts so far this year, with the Health Department attributing the current rise in H1N1 cases to the state’s usual seasonal pattern and urging people not to panic. According to surveillance data from the Integrated Health Information Platform (IHIP), 4,212 influenza cases had been confirmed in the state as of August 22, 2026. H1N1 is a strain of the influenza A virus that can cause seasonal flu. Common symptoms include fever, cough, sore throat, body ache and fatigue. Bengaluru accounts for the majority of the cases. The Greater Bengaluru Authority (MSU) area has reported 2,070 cases so far this year, compared to 2,587 in 2025 and 1,189 in 2024. Bengaluru Urban has recorded 1,011 cases, broadly comparable to 961 cases in 2025 and 991 in 2024. The Health Department said influenza generally records two seasonal peaks in Karnataka — between January and March and again between July and September. The current increase in cases therefore falls within the state's usual seasonal pattern. Health Department reviews preparedness Health Minister UT Khader chaired a review meeting with senior health officials from the state and districts to assess preparedness to manage the seasonal rise in influenza. The department said government health facilities have adequate infrastructure, essential medicines and other supplies to handle a possible increase in cases. Surveillance for Influenza-Like Illness (ILI) and Severe Acute Respiratory Infection (SARI) has also been strengthened in line with guidelines issued by the World Health Organization and the Union Ministry of Health and Family Welfare. Surveillance is being carried out through designated sentinel sites under the ICMR-NCDC network for pan-respiratory virus surveillance, as well as through the Viral Research and Diagnostic Laboratories (VRDL) network. The department said laboratories have sufficient consumables to ensure timely sample collection and testing. Health facilities have been directed to maintain adequate stocks of essential supplies, including personal protective equipment, N95 masks and Oseltamivir, an antiviral medication used to treat influenza. Healthcare workers have also been sensitised to identify ILI and SARI cases early, assess risk and provide appropriate treatment. items.title: ‘Victory of our protests’: Parandur protesters celebrate as CM Vijay scraps airport
items.summary: “This is the victory of our three-year-long protests,” Ekanapuram resident Janathanan told TNM on Monday, August 24, after Tamil Nadu Chief Minister C Joseph Vijay announced in the state Assembly that the Parandur airport project would be scrapped. “We are extremely happy and are planning celebrations this evening,” Janathanan added. The announcement brings to an end a three-year-long protest by residents of Ekanapuram and neighbouring villages, who opposed the project over the acquisition of farmland and the displacement of residents. Environmentalists had also objected to the project, warning that it would significantly impact the area’s water resources, which include many lakes and wetlands. Announcing the scrapping of the project, Vijay said the government would identify an alternative site for Chennai’s second airport. He said a few sites had already been identified and would be assessed through scientific studies and technical feasibility assessments before a final location is selected. The Chief Minister said Chennai’s existing Meenambakkam airport, operated by the Airports Authority of India (AAI), currently handles around 30 million passengers a year. Given the city’s growing needs, he said a second airport was necessary to meet increasing passenger demand and support commercial development. However, Vijay said the second airport should not affect farmers’ livelihoods or require residents to be evicted. He accused the previous Dravida Munnetra Kazhagam (DMK) government of choosing Parandur despite these concerns. “I visited Ekanapuram and other neighbouring villages in January last year and heard their demands,” Vijay told the Assembly.
